tips.title: The square root pattern
tips.body: Write **0, 1, 2, 3, 4**, square root each and halve: $0, \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, 1$. That is the sine row for $0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°$. **Cosine is the same list backwards.** Write it in the margin before you read a single question.

tips.title: Two triangles beat any mnemonic
tips.body: Half a **unit square** gives $45°$ with sides $1, 1, \sqrt{2}$. Half an **equilateral triangle of side 2** gives $30°$ and $60°$ with sides $1, \sqrt{3}, 2$. If you forget a value, draw the triangle: it takes ten seconds and cannot be misremembered.

tips.title: The shortest side faces the smallest angle
tips.body: Unsure whether $\sin 30°$ is $\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$? The side opposite $30°$ is the **shortest**, so the ratio must be the **smaller** number. $\dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5$ beside $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.87$ settles it.

tips.title: Square them and add
tips.body: $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ for **every** angle. If your pair of values does not square and add to 1, one of them is wrong. At $30°$: $\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4} = 1$.

steps.title: Five angles you have to know without a calculator
steps.body:
Most trigonometry is done on a calculator. Five angles are not.

Edexcel requires you to **know the exact values** of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ for $\theta = 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°$ and $90°$, and of $\tan\theta$ for $0°, 30°, 45°$ and $60°$. These appear on the **non-calculator** paper, and there is no way to work them out in the room except from the two triangles below.

**Exact** means as a fraction or a surd, never as a decimal. $\sin 60° = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is exact; $0.866$ is not, and will lose the mark.

There is no $\tan 90°$. As the angle approaches $90°$ the adjacent side shrinks towards zero, so the ratio grows without limit. Writing *not defined* is the answer.

check.prompt: Why must these values be given exactly rather than as decimals?
check.solution: $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is the **exact** value; 0.866 is a rounded approximation of it. The non-calculator paper asks for the exact form.

Decimals are harder to write than surds
A decimal is a rounded value, so it is not exact

steps.title: Where 45° comes from
steps.body:
Take a **square of side 1** and cut it along a diagonal. Each half is a right-angled triangle with two sides of 1, two angles of $45°$, and a hypotenuse found by Pythagoras:

$$1^2 + 1^2 = 2, \text{ so the hypotenuse is } \sqrt{2}$$

Now read the ratios straight off that triangle.

visuals.alt: A right-angled triangle from half a unit square, with the two shorter sides of length one, the hypotenuse root two, and the two other angles both forty five degrees

check.prompt: What is the exact value of $\tan 45°$?
check.solution: The two short sides of the triangle are both 1, so $\tan 45° = \dfrac{1}{1} = 1$.

steps.title: Where 30° and 60° come from
steps.body:
Take an **equilateral triangle of side 2**, so every angle is $60°$. Cut it down the middle. Each half has a base of **1**, a hypotenuse of **2**, an angle of $60°$ at the bottom and $30°$ at the top, and a height from Pythagoras:

$$2^2 - 1^2 = 3, \text{ so the height is } \sqrt{3}$$

Every exact value for $30°$ and $60°$ comes off this one triangle.

check.prompt: What is the exact value of $\sin 30°$?
check.solution: In the 30-60-90 triangle the side opposite $30°$ is 1 and the hypotenuse is 2, so $\sin 30° = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

steps.title: 0° and 90°, and the pattern in the table
steps.body:
The two ends of the table are not from a triangle. Imagine the angle **shrinking to nothing**: the opposite side vanishes, so $\sin 0° = 0$, while the adjacent side becomes the whole hypotenuse, so $\cos 0° = 1$. At $90°$ it is the other way round.

There is a pattern that makes the table easy to write out under pressure. Write $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ in a row, take the **square root** of each, and **divide by 2**:

$$\dfrac{\sqrt{0}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{1}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{4}}{2} = 0, \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, 1$$

That is $\sin 0°, \sin 30°, \sin 45°, \sin 60°, \sin 90°$ in order. Cosine is the **same list backwards**. Tangent is sine divided by cosine.

visuals.alt: A table showing the square root pattern that generates the sine values, with cosine as the same list reversed

check.prompt: What is the exact value of $\cos 0°$?
check.solution: As the angle shrinks to nothing the adjacent side becomes the whole hypotenuse, so $\cos 0° = 1$.

steps.title: Your turn: write the table from scratch
steps.body:
Do this without looking back.

1. Draw the two triangles: half a unit square, and half an equilateral triangle of side 2. Label every side.
2. From them, write the full table of $\sin$, $\cos$ and $\tan$ for $0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°$.
3. Use the square root pattern to check your sine row.
4. Work out $4 \sin 60°$ and $\dfrac{\sin 60°}{\cos 60°}$, both exactly.

The second of those has a shortcut worth spotting.

steps.title: Going deeper: keeping it exact all the way
steps.body:
The marks at this level go to answers that stay exact from start to finish.

**Never convert to a decimal part way.** $\sin 60° = 0.866$ then multiplying gives a rounded answer that cannot be un-rounded. Keep $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and simplify at the end.

**Rationalise when asked.** $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ are the same number; multiply top and bottom by $\sqrt{2}$ to move between them. Both are usually accepted, but *give your answer in the form $a\sqrt{b}$* means rationalise.

**Two identities worth knowing**, because they turn up as *show that* questions:

- $\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta$
- $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$, which is Pythagoras in disguise

Check the second at $30°$: $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4} = 1$.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- You must know $\sin$ and $\cos$ for $0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°$, and $\tan$ for $0°, 30°, 45°, 60°$, **without a calculator**.
- **Exact** means a fraction or a surd. A decimal is a rounded value and loses the mark.
- $45°$ comes from **half a unit square**: sides $1, 1, \sqrt{2}$.
- $30°$ and $60°$ come from **half an equilateral triangle of side 2**: sides $1, \sqrt{3}, 2$.
- The sine row is $\dfrac{\sqrt{0}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{1}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{4}}{2}$. Cosine is the **same list backwards**.
- $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, and $\tan 90°$ is **not defined**.
- $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ for every angle.
- Keep everything exact to the last line: $10\cos 30° = 5\sqrt{3}$, not $8.66$.

visuals.alt: A summary table of the exact trigonometric values with the two triangles they come from

questions.prompt: What is the exact value of $\sin 30°$?
questions.solution: From the 30-60-90 triangle, the side opposite $30°$ is 1 and the hypotenuse is 2, so $\sin 30° = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.prompt: What is the exact value of $\tan 45°$?
questions.solution: The two short sides of the 45-45-90 triangle are equal, so $\tan 45° = \dfrac{1}{1} = 1$.

questions.prompt: What is the exact value of $\cos 60°$?
questions.solution: The side next to $60°$ is 1 and the hypotenuse is 2, so $\cos 60° = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the exact value of $\sin 60°$?
questions.solution: $\sin 60° = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. The decimal 0.866 is a rounded value, not an exact one.

questions.prompt: Work out the exact value of $2 \sin 30°$.
What is the exact value of $\tan 60°$?
questions.solution: In the 30-60-90 triangle, opposite over adjacent at $60°$ is $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{1} = \sqrt{3}$.
As the angle approaches $90°$ the **adjacent** side shrinks towards zero, and dividing by something approaching zero grows without limit. So there is no value.

questions.prompt: Which of the five angles gives the same value for sine and cosine?
questions.solution: At $45°$ the triangle is symmetrical, so $\sin 45° = \cos 45° = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. It is the only one of the five.

questions.solution: 0.87 is a **rounded** value of $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Using it makes every later step approximate, and a question asking for an exact answer will not accept the result.

questions.prompt: Work out the exact value of $4 \sin 30° + 2 \cos 60°$.
Show how the exact values of $\sin 30°$, $\cos 30°$ and $\tan 30°$ can be found from an equilateral triangle.
questions.solution: Start with an equilateral triangle of side two, so every angle is sixty degrees. Cut it in half down the middle, from one vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. That line splits the sixty degree angle at the top into two thirties, and meets the base at a right angle, so each half is a right-angled triangle with an angle of thirty degrees at the top and sixty at the bottom. The base of each half is one, since the original side of two has been halved, and the hypotenuse is still two. By Pythagoras the height is the square root of two squared minus one squared, which is the square root of three. Now read the ratios at the thirty degree angle. The opposite side is one and the hypotenuse is two, so sine of thirty is one half. The adjacent side is root three and the hypotenuse is two, so cosine of thirty is root three over two. Opposite over adjacent gives tangent of thirty as one over root three.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Start with an equilateral triangle of side 2**, so every angle is $60°$.

**Cut it in half** from one vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. That line splits the $60°$ angle into two $30°$ angles and meets the base at a **right angle**.

Each half therefore has:

- base $= 1$, since the side of 2 has been halved
- hypotenuse $= 2$, unchanged
- height $= \sqrt{2^2 - 1^2} = \sqrt{3}$, by Pythagoras

**Read the ratios at the $30°$ angle:**

$$\sin 30° = \dfrac{1}{2} \qquad \cos 30° = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \qquad \tan 30° = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$$

questions.prompt: A right-angled triangle has a hypotenuse of 12 cm and an angle of 60°. Find both other sides exactly, and verify your answers with Pythagoras.
questions.solution: The side opposite the sixty degree angle is twelve times sine of sixty, which is twelve times root three over two, giving six root three centimetres. The side adjacent to it is twelve times cosine of sixty, which is twelve times one half, giving six centimetres. To verify, six squared is thirty six and six root three squared is thirty six times three, which is one hundred and eight. Adding them gives one hundred and forty four, which is twelve squared, so the three sides are consistent.

markScheme.description: uses 12 sin 60° for the opposite side

criteria.text: Uses 12 sin 60° for the side opposite the 60 degree angle
Gives that side exactly as 6√3 cm
Gives the other side as 6 cm from 12 cos 60°

questions.modelAnswer:
**The side opposite $60°$:**

$$12 \sin 60° = 12 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \mathbf{6\sqrt{3}} \text{ cm}$$

**The side adjacent to $60°$:**

$$12 \cos 60° = 12 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \mathbf{6} \text{ cm}$$

**Check with Pythagoras:**

$$6^2 + (6\sqrt{3})^2 = 36 + 108 = 144 = 12^2$$

Note that $6\sqrt{3}$ must be left as a surd. Writing 10.39 would not be exact.

examTechnique.body:
Write the table out in the margin the moment the paper starts, before you have read a question. It takes twenty seconds using the square root pattern and it removes all the recall pressure.

The pattern: write 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, square root each and divide by 2. That is the sine row. Cosine is the same list backwards. Tangent is sine divided by cosine.

Keep everything exact to the last line. The moment you write 0.866 you have lost the exact answer and cannot get it back.

If the question says *give your answer in the form $a\sqrt{b}$*, rationalise the denominator: multiply top and bottom by the surd.

Draw the two triangles if you are unsure of a value. Half a unit square gives 45 degrees; half an equilateral triangle of side 2 gives 30 and 60. Both take seconds and cannot be misremembered.

Check with Pythagoras when you have found two sides. It costs one line and catches a swapped sine and cosine.
examinerErrors: Giving a decimal when the question asked for an exact value.
Swapping sine and cosine for 30 and 60 degrees, which the triangle would have settled.
Writing a value for tan 90 degrees. It is not defined.
Leaving an answer as 8 over root 2 when the question asked for the form a root b.
Rounding part way through, so the final answer is no longer exact.
Using the calculator on a non-calculator paper question and losing the exact form.
Mixing up which side is opposite and which is adjacent for the angle being used.
Squaring a surd wrongly: root 3 all squared is 3, not 9.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer writes the table out before starting and works entirely in surds, converting to a decimal only if asked. It knows both triangles well enough to rebuild any value, and says which one a value came from when explaining. It rationalises a denominator without being told when the answer is requested in the form a root b, and checks a pair of sides against Pythagoras. On a show that question it derives the value from the triangle rather than quoting it, and uses the identity sin squared plus cos squared equals one as a check rather than a decimal approximation.
